label: Go (Fresher)
blurb: Go interview prep for 0–2 YOE: Go syntax, structs, interfaces, goroutines, channels, error handling, slices, maps, basic HTTP servers, testing, and Go modules — the questions every entry-level Go interview covers.
audience: 0–2 YOE Go developers, fresh graduates learning Go, engineers switching to Go from Python/Java/JavaScript

modules.title: Go Syntax & Language Fundamentals
modules.intro: Go syntax interview questions are the first thing every interviewer reaches for when screening a Go fresher. This module covers the building blocks of the Go language — how Go's type system works (every variable has a type, zero values mean no uninitialized state), the short variable declaration := vs var (and when each is used), all basic types (bool, int, float64, string, byte, rune), constants including the iota enumerator pattern, Go's single loop construct for (for loop, while-style for, range loop), switch without fallthrough by default, basic pointer syntax (the & address-of operator, the * dereference operator — and why Go pointers are safer than C pointers), and the blank identifier _ for discarding values. Every answer explains the design decision behind the feature — why Go has only one loop construct, why zero values eliminate a class of bugs — so you understand not just the syntax but the reasoning interviewers expect you to articulate.

modules.title: Functions, Closures & Variadic
modules.intro: Go functions are first-class values — you can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. This module covers Go's function syntax (named functions vs anonymous function literals), multiple return values (the Go idiom of returning a result and an error together — (value, error)), named return values and why they are sometimes useful and sometimes confusing, closures in Go (how a function literal captures variables from its enclosing scope, the loop variable capture gotcha that catches everyone once), variadic functions (the ...T syntax, how to spread a slice into a variadic call), defer (how deferred calls execute LIFO at function return, the argument evaluation timing — a common interview trick question), and panic/recover as the last-resort mechanism for genuinely unrecoverable errors. These fundamentals underpin every pattern in more advanced Go code.

modules.title: Structs, Methods & Interfaces Basics
modules.intro: Structs and interfaces are Go's answer to classes and inheritance — and the interview question 'how does Go do OOP?' is one every Go fresher faces. This module covers struct definition and initialisation (named fields, positional literals, the zero-value struct), value receivers vs pointer receivers (when a method should take *T vs T, the rule of thumb: mutating methods take a pointer receiver, read-only methods can take either, but be consistent on a type), the method set rules (value T includes value-receiver methods; *T includes both), interfaces in Go (defining an interface with one or more method signatures), implicit satisfaction (a type satisfies an interface by having the right methods — no 'implements' keyword needed), and struct embedding as Go's composition mechanism. Every answer addresses the comparison to Java/Python classes that interviewers expect you to articulate: 'Go doesn't have inheritance — what does it have instead and why is that a good thing?'

modules.title: Strings, Runes & Type Conversions
modules.intro: Strings in Go work differently from Python or Java, and every fresher interview includes at least one string question. This module covers string immutability in Go (a string is a read-only slice of bytes — you cannot modify it in place), the distinction between byte (uint8, raw bytes) and rune (int32, a Unicode code point — ranging over a string with range gives runes, not bytes), safe string iteration with range (iterates runes), the strings package for common operations (strings.Contains, strings.Split, strings.TrimSpace, strings.Builder for efficient concatenation), strconv for converting between strings and numbers (strconv.Atoi, strconv.Itoa, strconv.ParseFloat), explicit type conversion with T(x) syntax (Go has no implicit numeric conversions), and type assertions for interface values. The gotcha question: 'why does len("café") return 5 instead of 4?' — this module answers it and explains why.

modules.title: Slices, Maps & Arrays
modules.intro: Slices and maps are the workhorse data structures in Go, and the interview questions around them test whether you understand what's happening under the hood. This module covers the array vs slice distinction (arrays have fixed length at compile time and are value types; slices are descriptors pointing to an underlying array), the three-field slice header (pointer, len, cap), append and what happens when capacity is exceeded (a new, larger array is allocated and the slice descriptor is updated — why this means append can return a different backing array), the common slice tricks (copy, delete element by index, two-pointer for filter-in-place), maps with make and map literals, map zero values (reading a missing key returns the zero value; writing to a nil map panics — the check-existence idiom: v, ok := m[k]), safe concurrent map access (sync.Map or map + Mutex), and ranging over slices and maps. Every answer includes the gotcha the interviewer is testing.

modules.title: Error Handling in Go
modules.intro: Go error handling is explicit by design — there is no try/catch, no exceptions, and errors are values that flow through the program like any other return value. This module introduces the error interface (one method: Error() string), creating errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, the ubiquitous (value, error) return pattern and the if err != nil idiom, wrapping errors with the %w verb in fmt.Errorf (Go 1.13+), creating custom error types by implementing the error interface, and the critical distinction between panic (for programmer errors and truly unrecoverable states) and the error return value (for expected error conditions like 'file not found' or 'user not found'). The comparison question is always 'why doesn't Go have exceptions?' and this module gives the answer Go's designers intended: explicit error handling makes error paths visible, forces callers to handle them, and makes code easier to reason about.

modules.title: Goroutines & Channels Basics
modules.intro: Goroutines and channels are the two features that make Go famous for concurrency, and they come up in every Go fresher interview. This module covers goroutine creation (the go keyword before a function call — that is all you need to start a new goroutine), why goroutines are lightweight (they start at about 2 KB of stack, grow dynamically, and are scheduled by the Go runtime — not the OS), the channel data type (typed conduits for communicating between goroutines), creating channels with make(chan T) for unbuffered and make(chan T, n) for buffered, sending and receiving (ch <- value to send, value := <-ch to receive), how unbuffered channels synchronise sender and receiver (both block until the other is ready), buffered channels (sender only blocks when buffer is full, receiver only blocks when buffer is empty), closing a channel (signals no more values will be sent; receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value), and ranging over a channel until it's closed. Every answer uses a runnable example and addresses the comparison: 'goroutines vs threads.'

modules.title: Basic Synchronisation in Go
modules.intro: Basic synchronisation in Go covers the tools you need to coordinate goroutines safely. This module covers sync.WaitGroup for waiting on a group of goroutines (Add before launching, Done with defer in each goroutine, Wait to block until all finish — and the off-by-one mistake that causes panics), sync.Mutex for protecting shared state from concurrent access (Lock/Unlock, defer mu.Unlock() as the safe pattern), the data race definition (two goroutines accessing the same variable concurrently with at least one write — undefined behaviour in Go), the -race flag for detecting races in tests, the select statement for listening on multiple channels simultaneously (how the runtime picks randomly when multiple cases are ready, the default case for non-blocking channel operations), and the done-channel pattern for signalling goroutine shutdown. For freshers, the take-away is: prefer communicating over sharing state, but know the sync primitives when you need them.

modules.title: File I/O & Standard Packages
modules.intro: File I/O in Go is built on the io.Reader and io.Writer interfaces — two of the most important interfaces in the Go standard library. This module covers os.ReadFile and os.WriteFile for simple whole-file operations, os.Open and os.Create for streaming large files (the defer f.Close() pattern — forgetting this leaks a file descriptor), bufio.Scanner for reading a file line by line without loading it all into memory, bufio.Writer for buffered writes (fewer syscalls), the io.Reader and io.Writer interfaces (what makes them powerful: any type that implements Read([]byte)(int, error) can be used as a Reader — files, network connections, in-memory buffers, HTTP response bodies all satisfy the interface), io.Copy for efficiently copying between a Reader and Writer, the filepath package for platform-independent path manipulation, and reading environment variables with os.Getenv. These I/O patterns appear in real Go services and in coding interviews.

modules.title: JSON Encoding & Basic HTTP
modules.intro: JSON and basic HTTP are the two standard library features every Go fresher uses on day one. This module covers encoding/json for serialisation (json.Marshal a struct → JSON bytes, json.Unmarshal JSON bytes → struct), struct tags for controlling JSON field names (json:"field_name" and json:"field,omitempty" to omit zero values), common gotchas (unexported fields are silently ignored, json.Number for avoiding float64 precision loss on large integers, map[string]interface{} as the catch-all for unknown JSON), the net/http client for making HTTP requests (http.Get, http.Post, the critical must-close-response-body pattern with defer resp.Body.Close()), reading the response body with io.ReadAll, and building a simple HTTP server (http.HandleFunc, http.ListenAndServe, reading request body and query params, writing a JSON response). These are the building blocks every Go service is made from.

modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithms in Go
modules.intro: Data structures and algorithms interview questions in Go test both your CS fundamentals and your knowledge of Go's standard library. This module covers Big-O complexity for Go's built-in operations (slice append amortised O(1), map lookup/insert O(1), len() O(1) for slices and maps), implementing a stack and queue using a slice (Go has no built-in stack/queue — slices serve both roles with append and slice re-assignment), implementing a singly linked list as a Go struct, sorting with sort.Slice (the comparator function) and sort.Strings / sort.Ints for common cases, binary search with sort.Search, the two-pointer pattern for array problems (written idiomatically in Go), and hash map patterns for frequency counting and two-sum style problems. Every answer shows the complete, runnable Go code the interviewer expects — not pseudocode, not Python with Go syntax bolted on, but idiomatic Go using range, multiple assignment, and the standard library tools Go developers actually reach for.

modules.title: Testing Package Basics
modules.intro: Testing in Go is built into the standard library and the toolchain — you do not need a testing framework to write good tests. This module covers the _test.go file naming convention (only compiled during test runs), the TestXxx naming rule (must start with Test, take *testing.T, return nothing), t.Error and t.Logf for reporting failures without stopping the test vs t.Fatal and t.Fatalf for stopping immediately (the distinction matters when you have multiple assertions), the table-driven test pattern (a slice of struct test cases — the idiomatic Go way to avoid duplicated test functions), running tests with go test ./..., go test -v for verbose output, go test -run TestFunctionName to run a specific test, go test -cover for coverage reporting, and example functions (ExampleFunctionName runs as a test and doubles as documentation). These basics cover 80% of what Go freshers need to write and understand tests in a Go codebase.

modules.title: Go Modules & go.mod
modules.intro: Go modules are how Go manages dependencies, and understanding go.mod is essential for working in any Go codebase. This module covers the module declaration in go.mod (module path convention — typically a GitHub URL like github.com/yourname/myapp), packages and imports (each directory is a package; the package name is declared at the top of every .go file; import paths are module-path + directory path), exported vs unexported identifiers (capitalised name = exported, accessible from other packages; lowercase = package-private), adding dependencies with go get (updates go.mod and go.sum), go mod tidy (removes unused dependencies, adds missing ones — the command you run before committing), the go.sum file (cryptographic hash of every dependency — always commit it), and the standard project layout conventions (cmd/ for entry points, internal/ for private code, pkg/ for reusable libraries). The interview question: 'what is the difference between go.mod and go.sum?'

modules.title: Building HTTP Servers in Go
modules.intro: Building HTTP servers in Go is straightforward with the standard library, and it is the first thing every Go web developer learns. This module covers http.HandleFunc for registering handlers (the function signature func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)), http.ListenAndServe to start the server, reading the request (r.URL.Query() for query params, r.PathValue() for path params in Go 1.22+, json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&struct) for JSON request body), writing responses (w.Header().Set() for headers, w.WriteHeader() for status codes, json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(&struct) for JSON responses), basic middleware (a function that wraps an http.Handler — the logging middleware pattern), Go 1.22's enhanced ServeMux (method + path routing without a third-party router), and a brief introduction to Gin as the most popular Go web framework and why you might reach for it. Every answer shows the complete, runnable code. The interview question: 'build a simple REST endpoint that accepts a JSON body and returns a JSON response.'

modules.title: Docker for Go (Basics)
modules.intro: Docker for Go fresher interviews covers what makes Go special in containerised environments. This module covers a basic Dockerfile for a Go application (FROM golang as builder, COPY go.mod go.sum, RUN go mod download, COPY ., RUN go build, then a minimal final stage), the Go multi-stage build pattern (why it produces a small image — the final stage only needs the compiled binary, not the Go toolchain), CGO_ENABLED=0 for building a fully static binary that runs in a scratch or distroless container, running the compiled Go binary in Docker (docker run, exposing ports, passing environment variables with -e), and Docker Compose for running a Go service with its dependencies (a simple compose file connecting a Go HTTP service to a PostgreSQL container). The interview question freshers encounter most: 'what is a multi-stage Docker build and why is Go particularly well-suited to it?'

modules.title: Cloud & Deployment Fundamentals for Go
modules.intro: Cloud and deployment fundamentals for Go freshers cover the patterns every Go developer encounters before they touch a cloud console. This module covers what makes Go binaries ideal for cloud deployment (statically compiled, no runtime dependency, fast startup — Go containers cold-start in under 100 ms vs JVM cold starts of 1–3 seconds), the twelve-factor app principles applied to Go services (configuration via environment variables, logs to stdout, stateless processes), implementing a /healthz health check endpoint (the Kubernetes readiness and liveness probe target), Kubernetes basics for Go developers (a Deployment YAML for a Go container, the readiness probe, resource requests and limits), reading configuration from environment variables in Go (os.Getenv, the envconfig library for struct-based config), and basic structured logging (log.Printf vs structured logs with log/slog for JSON output that log aggregators can parse). These basics give Go freshers the vocabulary to talk about their Go service in a production context.

modules.title: Common Go Interview Scenarios
modules.intro: Common Go interview scenarios for freshers are the practical 'what does this code do?' and 'spot the bug' questions that differentiate candidates who have written real Go from those who have only read about it. This module covers seven scenario categories: goroutine vs thread (when to use a goroutine, the classic 'print numbers 1 to 10 concurrently' problem and why it requires sync), channel direction (what does chan<- T mean in a function signature and why you'd use it), interface vs concrete type (when a function should accept an io.Writer vs a *os.File), pointer vs value receiver (the method set gotcha with pointer receivers and interface satisfaction), the nil map panic (writing to a nil map panics; reading returns zero — how to prevent both), defer ordering (LIFO execution, the argument evaluation timing that catches everyone), and error handling scenarios (when to return nil, when to wrap, when to use a sentinel). Every scenario is a runnable Go program the interviewer will put in front of you.

modules.title: Problem Solving & Coding Patterns in Go
modules.intro: Problem-solving and coding patterns in Go cover the programs every Go fresher is asked to write in a 30-minute screening. This module covers seven canonical problems written idiomatically in Go: FizzBuzz (the baseline — if it takes more than 3 minutes something is wrong, but showing clean switch and string conversion matters), Fibonacci (iterative with a simple loop vs recursive — and why iterative is preferred in Go for stack-depth reasons), palindrome check (rune-safe using a slice of runes, not indexing bytes), anagram check (using a frequency map with make(map[rune]int)), two-sum (the hash map approach, O(n) time — the Go map literal and the ok pattern for existence check), reverse a string rune-safely (range + append to a rune slice + string()), and word count (strings.Fields + a map, the range-over-string gotcha). Every solution is complete, compiles, and is written the way a Go developer writes it — not Java or Python style with Go syntax. The meta-lesson: interviewers watch how you use the language, not just whether you get the right answer.

modules.title: Database Basics in Go
modules.intro: Database interaction is tested in every Go fresher interview — Go engineers are expected to know both the stdlib database/sql approach and a lightweight ORM. This module covers how database/sql works (opening a DB connection, sql.Open vs ping, the driver registration pattern), executing SELECT queries and scanning rows correctly (the Row vs Rows difference, closing rows to avoid connection leaks), using prepared statements to prevent SQL injection, wrapping multiple operations in a transaction (Begin/Commit/Rollback), GORM model definitions and AutoMigrate, and configuring connection pool settings (SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, SetConnMaxLifetime). These are fresher interview staples at any Go backend role.
